title: Writing Your First Kernels
blurb: Tests the map pattern and the bounds check, SAXPY and sigmoid kernels, why the CPU won every single-shot SAXPY size, why amortising the transfer reversed it, the three timings a GPU decision needs, and when an operation is worth a kernel at all.

options: Each output depending on its neighbours, as in a stencil
One independent operation per element, no communication
Threads combining their results into one value, such as a sum
Threads sharing a tile of data through shared memory
questions.explanation: Map applies the same operation to every element on its own. Combining into one value is reduction, and neighbour-dependent outputs are stencils, both in Chapter 42.

questions.prompt: Why does Procedure 41.1 keep the if (i < n) check?
options: nvcc refuses to compile a kernel without an if statement.
Spare threads in the last block would run past the buffer.
It stops two threads from writing to the same element at once.
Without it, the kernel runs only on the first block of the grid.
questions.explanation: The last block has threads with i ≥ n. Without the check they read or write past the end, which is undefined behaviour, sometimes silent and sometimes a crash.

questions.prompt: n = 1,000 elements, launched with 256 threads per block and grid = (n + 255) / 256 in integer division. How many threads have i ≥ n and are stopped by the bounds check?
questions.explanation: grid = 1255 / 256 = 4 blocks, so 1,024 threads. 1,024 − 1,000 = 24 threads fall past the end.

options: The matrix product of x and y, in single precision
The dot product of x and y, summed into a single number
y = a·x + y, element by element, in single precision
y = x·y + a, with a different a for each element
questions.explanation: Single-precision A·X Plus Y: one multiply and one add per element. It mirrors the parameter update inside SGD-family optimisers.

refLinks.label: §41.2.1 SAXPY: The “Hello World” of Numerical Kernels

questions.prompt: How does the sigmoid kernel differ from the SAXPY kernel?
options: It needs shared memory to hold the exponentials between threads.
It needs a grid-stride loop, since expf is too slow for one pass.
Only the body inside if (i < n). The shape is the same.
It must run on Tensor Cores, since expf is a matrix operation.
questions.explanation: The chapter stresses the map pattern carries over unchanged. Every elementwise activation, ReLU, GELU, sigmoid or tanh, is the same kernel with a different body.

questions.prompt: In the sigmoid kernel, what is expf()?
options: A host function the kernel calls back to on the CPU
A lookup table of e^x values loaded from global memory
CUDA's device-side single-precision exponential
The double-precision exponential, rounded to float at the end
questions.explanation: expf is the float version of exp, available in device code. Kernels can't call host functions.

questions.prompt: Why did the CPU win every single-shot SAXPY size, from 1,000 to 100 million?
options: The GPU was still warming up during every timed run.
Transfers cost far more than SAXPY's tiny arithmetic.
The GPU kernel was written incorrectly and ran on one thread.
The CPU used Tensor Cores, which the GPU kernel didn't.
questions.explanation: A single round trip pays the full transfer every time, and SAXPY does too little work per byte to make up for it. The chapter says this is not an experimental mistake.

refLinks.label: §41.2.2 The Uncomfortable Result: the CPU Can Win

questions.prompt: What does the chapter call the most common way beginners misjudge GPU performance?
options: Running the kernel twice and averaging the two times
Writing kernels in C++ instead of Python
Benchmarking on a GPU with far too many SMs for the size of the problem
Timing a one-shot round trip and expecting the GPU to win
questions.explanation: A one-shot benchmark with transfers can make the "obviously faster" GPU lose. The fix is to measure the scenario the real workload has.

refLinks.label: §41.2.2 The Uncomfortable Result: the CPU Can Win

questions.prompt: What turned the SAXPY loss into a 30.2x GPU win?
options: Rewriting the kernel with float4 loads and __restrict__ pointers throughout
Moving from n = 10 million to n = 100 million
Running the same kernel 100 times on data moved to the GPU once
Using pinned memory for the single round trip
questions.explanation: Not one line of the kernel changed. One transfer in, 100 launches, one transfer out spread the transfer cost across all the calls.

refLinks.label: §41.2.3 The Fix Isn’t a Faster Kernel. It’s Amortisation

questions.prompt: Why does PyTorch keep tensors on the GPU for a whole training loop?
options: CPU memory is too small to hold model weights during training.
GPU tensors can't be moved back to the CPU until training ends.
Round trips between operations would make it slower overall.
Keeping tensors resident is a style convention with no speed effect.
questions.explanation: The chapter calls .to('cuda') once at the start "load-bearing for the entire performance case". The single-shot SAXPY result shows what happens otherwise.

refLinks.label: §41.2.3 The Fix Isn’t a Faster Kernel. It’s Amortisation

questions.prompt: The amortised GPU run took 10.94 ms for 100 SAXPY calls. What is the time per call in ms? Give four decimal places.
questions.explanation: 10.94 / 100 = 0.1094 ms per call, including one share of the single transfer in and out.

questions.prompt: The CPU took 330.70 ms for the same 100 calls. What is the GPU's speedup? Give one decimal place.
questions.explanation: 330.70 / 10.94 = 30.2. In the single-shot run at the same n, the CPU won by about 4x (2.14 ms against 8.63 ms).

questions.prompt: Which timings does Procedure 41.2 say a real GPU-against-CPU decision needs? Select all that apply.
options: The CPU baseline
The GPU time per call with data resident across many calls
The GPU kernel time alone, with no transfers in any scenario
The GPU round trip for a single call
questions.explanation: Compare single-shot work against the round trip and repeated work against the amortised time. Kernel time alone hides transfer costs that the real workload will pay.

questions.prompt: worth_gpu_kernel in Listing 41.3 gets n_elements = 5,000,000, flops_per_element = 2, will_stay_resident = False and expected_call_count = 1. What does it return?
options: False
True
It raises an error
None
questions.explanation: Not resident, so the first branch is skipped. n is above 100,000, so the second is skipped too. flops per element is 2, below 5, so it returns False: too cheap to survive a single-shot round trip, like SAXPY.

questions.prompt: worth_gpu_kernel gets n_elements = 2,000,000, flops_per_element = 40, will_stay_resident = False and expected_call_count = 1. What does it return, and what does that mean?
options: None, meaning the case is ambiguous and both paths should be benchmarked
False, meaning a single call can never be worth a GPU kernel
True, meaning a GPU kernel will win, so no benchmark is needed at this size
None, meaning the inputs were invalid and the function gave up
questions.explanation: All three early checks fail: not resident, n above 100,000, flops at least 5. The function returns None for "genuinely ambiguous: benchmark both paths for real".

questions.prompt: A design doc reports a 30x GPU speedup for an operation that runs once per request on data arriving from the CPU. What is wrong, per Procedure 41.2?
options: Nothing. A 30x speedup holds for any workload that uses the same kernel.
The speedup is too low. Single-shot work is always faster than amortised.
The doc should report kernel time alone, which is the real speed of the GPU.
30x is amortised. Single-shot work needs the round-trip time.
questions.explanation: The procedure's common mistake is reporting amortised numbers for a single-shot use case. The two can differ by an order of magnitude in opposite directions, as SAXPY showed.

questions.prompt: At n = 100 million, single-shot SAXPY took 28.5 ms on the CPU and 85.9 ms on the GPU. How does the chapter sum it up?
options: The two are tied within measurement error.
The GPU finally wins once n passes 10 million.
The CPU still finishes in about a third of the GPU's total time.
The GPU kernel itself took most of the 85.9 ms, not the transfers.
questions.explanation: 28.5 / 85.9 ≈ 0.33. Even at the largest size, transfers dominate, so the CPU wins. The kernel is a small part of the GPU total, as in Chapter 39.

questions.prompt: What does the chapter's mental model compare a GPU kernel to?
options: A courier who delivers every parcel to a different address
A specialist hired by the job, with a fixed booking fee that more work spreads thinner
A factory line that runs faster the more workers it has
A library where each book can be borrowed by one reader at a time
questions.explanation: The booking fee is the data transfer. One tiny task and the fee eats the budget. A hundred tasks in a row and it barely matters. That is amortisation.

bookExercises.prompt: In your own words, explain why a single-shot SAXPY round trip loses to a CPU loop at every size this chapter tested, using the transfer-vs-compute cost idea from Chapter 39.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: A single-shot SAXPY call pays the full host-to-device and device-to-host transfer cost for exactly one kernel launch's worth of work. SAXPY does only one multiply and one add per element, so the arithmetic is cheap relative to moving the array across PCIe twice. Per Chapter 39's lesson, the transfer, not the kernel, dominates total time, and no problem size closes that gap because both the transfer cost and the compute cost scale together with `n`.

bookExercises.prompt: Define "amortisation" as this chapter uses it, and state which single measurement changed between the single-shot and the 100-repeated-call SAXPY experiments.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Amortisation is spreading a fixed one-time cost, here, the host-to-device and device-to-host transfer, across many repeated operations so its per-operation share shrinks. The single measurement that changed between the two SAXPY experiments was how many kernel launches occurred per data transfer: one in the single-shot case, one hundred in the amortised case. The kernel code, the GPU, and the per-call problem size were identical in both.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 41.1 as a template, write the kernel body for a ReLU activation (`out[i] = max(0, in[i])`), and state which of this chapter's two example kernels (SAXPY or sigmoid) it more closely resembles in arithmetic cost per element.

This chapter measured a 30.2x amortised speedup at 100 repeated calls on `n = 10,000,000`. Using the single-shot table's `n = 10,000,000` row (CPU 2.1380 ms, GPU 8.6309 ms), estimate roughly how many repeated calls it would take for the amortised GPU total to first drop below the single-shot CPU time, assuming the GPU's per-call time stays close to the measured 0.1094 ms amortised figure.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: At `n = 10,000,000`, single-shot GPU total was 8.6309 ms and single-shot CPU total was 2.1380 ms: the GPU is roughly 4x slower single-shot. With amortised GPU time approaching about 0.1094 ms/call (from the 100-repeated-call measurement) and single-shot CPU at 2.1380 ms as the target to beat, even a single amortised GPU call (0.1094 ms, ignoring the one-time transfer already paid) is far below the CPU's 2.1380 ms. The crossover happens almost immediately after the transfer is paid once, consistent with the measured 30.2x speedup by 100 calls. The dominant cost being amortised away is the transfer, not the kernel, so the crossover point is set mainly by how large the one-time transfer cost is relative to the ~0.1 ms per-call kernel cost.

bookExercises.prompt: Run Listing 41.3 with `n_elements=500_000`, `flops_per_element=1`, `will_stay_resident=False`, `expected_call_count=1`. State what it returns and whether that matches this chapter's single-shot SAXPY finding.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: With `n_elements=500_000` (not `< 100_000`) and `flops_per_element=1` (`< 5`), the function returns `False`. This matches this chapter's single-shot SAXPY finding. SAXPY does 2 FLOPs/element (one multiply, one add), similarly low arithmetic intensity, and the CPU won at every size tested for exactly the same reason the heuristic flags: too little arithmetic per element to survive a single-shot round trip.

bookExercises.prompt: A colleague wants to port a CPU function that runs once per user request, on a few thousand elements each time, to a CUDA kernel "because GPUs are faster." Using this chapter's Trade-offs section and Procedure 41.3, write the two or three sentences you'd say back.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: A function that runs once per user request on a few thousand elements is almost exactly this chapter's single-shot, small-`n` case, well under the roughly 100,000-element threshold where GPU overhead alone is likely to dominate, and with no repeated calls to amortise the transfer against. Per this chapter's measured SAXPY sweep, the CPU should be assumed faster until proven otherwise by an actual benchmark (Procedure 41.2). Porting this to CUDA without measuring first would very likely make it slower, not faster.

bookExercises.prompt: Propose one realistic ML workload (in a sentence or two) where the single-shot SAXPY result, CPU wins, would be the *right* choice to design around, rather than something to "fix" by moving to GPU.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: A one-off batch script that loads a CSV, computes a single derived column once, and writes the result back out is a reasonable case where CPU is the right design choice. The data starts and ends on the host, the operation runs exactly once, and there is no repeated-call structure to amortise a transfer against, exactly the single-shot SAXPY shape this chapter measured losing to CPU at every tested size.

bookExercises.prompt: Read the "Maximizing Utilization" chapter of the NVIDIA CUDA C++ Best Practices Guide, focusing on CUDA streams. Summarise, in a few sentences, how overlapping transfer with compute could change this chapter's single-shot SAXPY result, and why it wouldn't fully close the gap for an operation this cheap per element.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Discussion only, no single answer expected. CUDA streams let a program overlap a kernel's compute with the *next* chunk's transfer, effectively hiding transfer latency behind computation happening concurrently. For an operation as arithmetically cheap as SAXPY, though, the kernel itself takes a tiny fraction of the total pipeline time (Chapter 39's vector-add pipeline showed the kernel under roughly 1% of total time). There is very little compute to overlap the transfer *against*, so streams would narrow but not eliminate the gap between single-shot GPU and CPU time for an operation this cheap per element. Streams help more for pipelines with a better balance of transfer and compute time.
